title: Iran Threatens NATO's Southeast Flank as War Nears Europe, US-Pakistan Spat Erupts Over Kashmir Visit
subhead: Tehran warns it will strike Bulgaria's Bezmer Air Base and other European targets aiding US operations, while Washington pivots from military to economic pressure on Iran. Separately, a Trump envoy's Kashmir visit strains US-Pakistan ties.

sections.heading: Iran Threatens Europe's Southeast as War Nears NATO's Flank
sections.body:
Iran has warned it will treat any country aiding US 'aggression' as a legitimate target, with southeastern Europe now in Tehran's crosshairs. According to Al Jazeera, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told his Bulgarian counterpart that nations supporting US military operations against Iran would face retaliation, and a Financial Times report citing unnamed Iranian sources said Tehran would consider attacking Europe if Washington escalates the conflict.

The threat centers on Bulgaria's Bezmer Air Base, which Sofia approved in July for refuelling US military aircraft supporting operations in the Middle East. Analysts cited by Al Jazeera note the region hosts multiple NATO bases, sits on the Black Sea, and serves as a key supply corridor for Ukraine. Armida van Rij of the Centre for European Reform called southeastern Europe 'the soft underbelly of Europe.' Iran has also reportedly attempted strikes as far as the joint US-UK base on Diego Garcia, 3,780 kilometres away.
sections.whyItMatters: A strike on NATO territory would be a major escalation, forcing the alliance to decide whether Article 5 applies and testing whether the Iran war can be contained to the Middle East.

sections.heading: Pezeshkian Calls for Ending War as US Shifts to Economic Pressure
sections.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday it is time to end the months-long war with the United States 'from a position of strength,' telling doctors that 'the whole world acknowledges our victory.' He defended the June memorandum of understanding against hardline critics, insisting it contained no concessions. Meanwhile, Omani and Iranian foreign ministers held a call on resuming dialogue and navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Oman's state news agency.

Washington is moving toward economic rather than military pressure. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned he will 'collapse' the Iranian government and will outline planned sanctions at a Monday news conference. President Trump expressed scepticism about Tehran's willingness to negotiate, saying 'they're not ready to make the right deal.' US media report the navy is protecting secret tanker convoys through the strait's southern sector, enabling 5-10 million barrels a day of exports.
sections.whyItMatters: The war is nearing the six-month mark with both sides signalling a desire to de-escalate, but the US pivot to sanctions and Iran's insistence on negotiating from strength leave the path to a deal uncertain.

sections.heading: US Re-Designates Hezbollah as Iranian Proxy, Sanctions Funding Network
sections.body:
The US Treasury has changed Hezbollah's legal designation from a 'terrorist organisation' to that of an Iranian proxy, calling the Lebanon-based group 'an extension' of the IRGC's Quds Force. A State Department official said the move reflects that Hezbollah 'operates with little to no regard for Lebanese sovereignty' and is 'not a Lebanese resistance movement.'

Washington also sanctioned 10 people in an alleged cash-transfer network, which the Treasury says Turkish businessman Yunus Alper Yilmaz leads, using couriers on commercial flights between Lebanon, Turkiye, the UAE and Iran to move 'hundreds of millions of dollars' outside the formal financial system. The re-designation comes as the US mediates stalled Israel-Lebanon negotiations.
sections.whyItMatters: The re-designation legally reframes Hezbollah as an arm of Iran's military, broadening the legal basis for sanctions and potentially complicating any Lebanon settlement.

sections.heading: Ukraine War Grinds On: Russian Social Crisis Warning, Kyiv Hits Fuel Supplies
sections.body:
Russia's ballistic missile campaign is causing record civilian deaths in Ukrainian cities, with the UN reporting 437 civilians killed in July, the highest since May 2022. Ukraine has run out of Patriot interceptors and cannot stop incoming ballistic missiles, though it still intercepts 90 percent of cruise missiles and drones. Ukrainian military intelligence says Russia has brought in an additional 50 North Korean weapons.

Ukraine's long-range strikes have destroyed Russian fuel and ammunition supplies, and a top Russian expert warned of impending social unrest as the economy struggles. Russia said it is ready for 'new ideas' on the war that match Putin's goals, while Ukraine's ex-defence chief has called for a wartime presidential election, adding pressure on Zelenskyy.
sections.whyItMatters: Both sides face mounting internal strain — Ukraine from civilian losses and recruitment violence, Russia from economic and social pressure — even as neither shows willingness to compromise.

sections.heading: US-Pakistan Spat Erupts Over Trump Envoy's Kashmir Visit
sections.body:
Pakistan's Foreign Ministry summoned the top US diplomat in Islamabad on Wednesday after US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, who also serves as Trump's special envoy for South and Central Asia, described Indian-administered Kashmir as 'an important part of India' during his first visit to the territory. Islamabad rejected the remark and reasserted Kashmir's status as disputed territory.

The visit was the first standalone trip by a serving US ambassador to Indian-administered Kashmir since 2019, when India stripped the territory of its autonomy. It comes at a delicate moment as Pakistan courts the Trump administration more closely than in years while Washington balances that against its strategic partnership with India.
sections.whyItMatters: The episode exposes the difficulty of Washington's dual-track approach to two nuclear-armed rivals, and any perceived tilt toward India could push Pakistan further from US alignment.

sections.heading: Bangladesh Holds First Contested Presidential Vote in 35 Years
sections.body:
Bangladesh has elected Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, a ruling-party veteran, as president by parliamentary vote, filling the vacancy left by Shahabuddin's resignation. The vote was the first contested presidential election in 35 years, pitting Alamgir against Oli Ahmad, nominee of the Jamaat-led 11-party alliance.

The transition comes six months into Prime Minister Tariq Rahman's term, with the government facing an energy crisis, rising prices and youth-led pressure for jobs. Al Jazeera reports the new administration is under strain as it navigates economic challenges.
sections.whyItMatters: A contested presidential vote signals a maturing of Bangladesh's political system in a strategically located South Asian state, though economic pressures will test the new leadership's stability.

bottomLine: The Iran-US war is entering a new phase: Tehran is threatening NATO's European flank even as both sides signal openness to ending the conflict, with Washington pivoting to a sanctions campaign and Iran insisting it negotiates from strength. The US re-designation of Hezbollah as an Iranian proxy widens the legal and financial front, while a Trump envoy's Kashmir remarks strain US-Pakistan ties and Bangladesh holds its first contested presidential vote in decades. The central question is whether the war can be contained to the Middle East or whether Europe's southeast becomes the next front.
